FrMS88-de5816-d1e111.summary: Poses the sixteenth question: whether abstractive knowledge of the divine essence can be had on the side of the object without knowing that God exists. Notes that abstractive cognition abstracts from being and non-being, presence and absence, and other contradictory extremes, and announces some difficulties.
claims: Abstractive cognition abstracts from existence and presence.

FrMS88-de5816-d1e129.summary: First difficulty: whether abstractive cognition abstracts from the object's terminating it or not, so that it could exist without the object terminating it.

FrMS88-de5816-d1e140.summary: Some say yes, since only a fundamental respect of the act to the object need be posited when the object does not exist.
claims: Reported view: abstractive cognition requires only a fundamental respect to a non-existent object.

FrMS88-de5816-d1e147.summary: Others say it is unintelligible that there be an understanding in which nothing is understood, though they too hold that the object need not actually exist.
claims: Reported view: every act of understanding has an understood object, though it need not exist.

FrMS88-de5816-d1e155.summary: Second difficulty: whether it abstracts from per se and per accidens. Answers that what belongs per se can be known abstractively, but not what belongs per accidens, since the representative represents uniformly while accidents vary; so one cannot know abstractively whether a man is white.
claims: Abstractive cognition cannot reach accidental features, since its representative is invariant.

FrMS88-de5816-d1e173.summary: Raises a difficulty from astronomy, which seems abstractive yet knows the existence of eclipses through a representative. Replies that astronomy never demonstrates existence: there is no demonstration of contingents as contingent, and an eclipse at a given time is contingent, since an angel moves the heavens contingently and God can impede it, as when the sun stood still for Joshua, or at the Judgment, when all such demonstrations would conclude falsely.
claims: There is no demonstration of contingents as contingent.
Astronomical predictions of eclipses are contingent and can be impeded by God.

FrMS88-de5816-d1e195.summary: Concludes that the astronomer has no greater certainty than the geometer, who also abstracts; he demonstrates only aptitude, not existence — that something is naturally apt to happen.
claims: Astronomy demonstrates aptitude, not existence.

FrMS88-de5816-d1e204.summary: Objects that natural philosophy would then fail, since it demonstrates a first unmoved mover from contingent propositions about motion (Physics VIII). Replies that this is not strictly demonstrative but argumentative: it starts from motion as intuitively known, and every proposition, however contingent, is per se known if intuitively known; from it one argues that what moves is moved by itself or by another, until reaching something unmoved, since there is no infinite regress. Turning to the question, reports the view that the divine essence cannot be known quidditatively abstracted from existence, since existence belongs to its concept as necessary being and pure act.
claims: The proof of an unmoved mover is argumentative, starting from intuitively known motion.
Any contingent proposition known intuitively is per se known.
Reported view: existence belongs to the concept of the divine essence.

FrMS88-de5816-d1e243.summary: 'Our Doctor' (Scotus) holds the contrary: we can have knowledge of the divine essence abstracted from existence through a representative. The order between quiddity and existence where they are really distinct (in creatures), allowing one to be understood without the other, remains where they are distinct by reason (in God).
claims: The divine essence can be known abstractively without its existence.
The order of quiddity to existence persists in God as an order of reason.

FrMS88-de5816-d1e259.summary: Second argument: what is predicated quidditatively of something is per se known of it, but 'God exists' is not per se known, since it is demonstrated.
claims: 'God exists' is demonstrated and so not per se known; existence is not quidditative of God.

FrMS88-de5816-d1e267.summary: Meyronnes holds this conclusion but for additional reasons. First: nothing common is of the quiddity of the simply simple; the divine essence is simply simple and existence is common, so existence is not of its quiddity.
claims: Existence, being common, is not of the quiddity of the simply simple divine essence.

FrMS88-de5816-d1e280.summary: Second: items of the same formal notion keep their essential order wherever they are; quantity of power and existence are of the same notion in God and creatures and in creatures power precedes existence; since quantity of power, the prior, is not said in quid of the divine essence, neither is existence.
claims: Quantity of power precedes existence and is not said in quid of the divine essence.

FrMS88-de5816-d1e296.summary: Third: what is of the same formal notion has the same quidditative predicates; the divine intellect and ours are of the same formal notion; if existence were said in quid of the divine intellect, it would be of ours, which is false.
claims: If existence were quidditative of the divine intellect it would be quidditative of ours.

FrMS88-de5816-d1e307.summary: Fourth: when something is multiplied, what belongs to its quidditative concept is multiplied; there are several formal notions in God, so there would be several existences, which is false since there is one existence of all persons and notional items.
claims: There is one existence in God for all persons and notions.

FrMS88-de5816-d1e325.summary: Reply to the argument for the opposing view: necessity and existence are intrinsic modes.
claims: Existence and necessity in God are intrinsic modes, not quidditative content.

FrMS88-de5816.summary: The sixteenth question of the prologue asks whether abstractive knowledge of the divine essence can be had on the side of the object without knowing that God exists. Abstractive cognition abstracts from being and non-being, presence and absence, and other contradictory extremes. Meyronnes treats three difficulties: whether it abstracts from the object's actually terminating it (views differ); whether it abstracts from per se and per accidens (it reaches what belongs per se but not accidents, since a representative represents uniformly while accidents vary); and astronomy, which seems abstractive yet knows eclipses — he replies that astronomy demonstrates only aptitude, not existence, since contingent events like eclipses can be impeded (by God, as in Joshua's miracle, or at the Judgment), and that the natural philosopher's proof of an unmoved mover is not strictly demonstrative but argumentative, starting from motion known intuitively and therefore per se known. On the question, against those who hold that existence belongs to the concept of the divine essence (as necessary being and pure act), he sides with 'our Doctor' (Scotus) that the divine essence can be known abstracted from existence: the order of quiddity and existence that is real in creatures persists as an order of reason in God, and 'God exists' is demonstrated and so not per se known. He adds his own reasons: existence, being common, cannot be of the quiddity of the simply simple divine essence; quantity of power precedes existence and is not said in quid of the essence; if existence were said in quid of the divine intellect it would be of ours; and plural formal notions in God would yield plural existences. Existence and the like are intrinsic modes.
claims: Abstractive cognition reaches what belongs to a thing per se but not its accidents.
Astronomy demonstrates only the aptitude of events like eclipses, not their existence.
The proof of an unmoved mover is argumentative, starting from motion intuitively known.
The divine essence can be known abstractively without knowing that it exists.
Existence is not of the quiddity of the divine essence, though it is an intrinsic mode of it.
